implementation_notes: Swift's standard library absorbs the pattern into the type system: Range is half-open, ClosedRange is closed, PartialRangeFrom/PartialRangeThrough/PartialRangeUpTo are the open-ended forms, and all of them conform to RangeExpression, so contains(_:) and the pattern-match operator ~= work uniformly, while relative(to:) resolves a partial range against a collection. The same types are collection indices, so the closed/open distinction is enforced by the compiler when slicing arrays. Interval-to-interval overlap is still hand-written: Range<Bound> provides contains for a ClosedRange argument, but two half-open ranges are compared with lowerBound/upperBound by hand.
code_sketch:
let billing = t0..<t1                        // half-open
let wholeQuarter = t0...t1                   // closed
let fromThenOn: PartialRangeFrom<Date> = t2...

billing.contains(later)                      // RangeExpression.contains
if case t0... = someDate { }                 // ~= pattern matching

// interval-to-interval overlap is not in the stdlib:
let clash = a.lowerBound < b.upperBound && b.lowerBound < a.upperBound
pitfalls: Range and ClosedRange are distinct types with distinct subscripts: mixing them up inside a collection is usually a compile error, but a hand-written overlap helper that accepts both can shift a boundary by one element silently.

Range<Bound> is a Collection only when Bound: Strideable, so Range<Date> is a valid interval but not iterable while 1..<5 can be looped over - the same type name carries two very different capabilities.

Partial ranges have no storable upper (or lower) bound, so a model that must round-trip intervals through storage needs its own optional-endpoint representation, or a collection to resolve against via relative(to:).
Converting a ClosedRange to Range adds one to the upper bound (swift's implementation advances by 1), so ClosedRange(0...Int.max) traps at runtime because Int.max + 1 is not representable.

variants.name: Foundation DateInterval (closed, start + duration)
variants.implementation_notes: For time spans Foundation provides DateInterval, documented as the closed interval [startDate, endDate] with start, end and duration, plus intersects(_:), intersection(with:) and contains(_:); it rejects reverse intervals by construction. Prefer it when the domain is exactly a closed date period and Foundation is already linked, and note that its closed convention differs from Range<Date>'s half-open one - a codebase that mixes both must convert deliberately, usually by advancing the end by one step.
variants.code_sketch:
let q1 = DateInterval(start: startOfQ1, end: startOfQ2)
q1.contains(someDate)
q1.intersects(otherInterval)
q1.intersection(with: otherInterval)

let day = DateInterval(start: startOfDay, duration: 86_400)   // end = start + duration
pitfalls: DateInterval is closed on both ends while Date-based Range is half-open, so the same period expressed in the two types differs by the end instant - the classic off-by-one-day bug when both are aggregated.

The start+duration initialiser recomputes end, and Foundation's date arithmetic is calendar-aware: a 24h duration across a DST change is not the same day boundary as start/end of the same calendar day.

Reverse intervals are unsupported (documented), so invalid input either fails construction or must be normalised before use - and an empty period (start == end) is allowed, which overlaps nothing but is not distinguishable from a zero-length window by type alone.
